column1: expanded-too-good-to-not-believe-cody-carnes|Jesus receives credit for healing and resurrection, and human power is expressly denied. The move from remembered wonders to certain future miracles needs a distinction between God's ability and a promise of a particular outcome.|The verses join testimony, dependence and praise; the bridge expands to restored families, freedom and public revival. The saving cross and repentance are not explained, so miracle testimony carries most of the argument.|The catalogue of concrete experiences gives the refrain content, but the repeated challenge can make questions about evidence sound like denial of God's power. These are different questions.|Divine power;Healing;Testimony;Revival|John 11:25;1 John 5:14;2 Corinthians 12:9|We've seen real life resurrection|This reports a specific kind of historical miracle. The lyric is testimony, not verification that the reported events occurred; it also does not promise a resurrection or healing on demand.|7,6,7

expanded-good-can-t-be-anything-else-cody-carnes|God's goodness is grounded in mercy, undeserved love and faithfulness amid uncertainty. Closed doors are included among his gifts, so goodness is not reduced to receiving every desired result.|The verses develop trust through remembered preservation and an uncertain future. Friendship and mercy add substance to the chorus, although Christ's saving work remains largely unstated.|The recurring goodness claim has a stable referent and clear contrasts. The hindsight image explains how trust grows through reflection without requiring every present event to feel good.|Divine goodness;Mercy;Trust;Providence|James 1:17;Psalm 23:6;Romans 8:28|||9,6,8

expanded-be-glad-cody-carnes|Praise answers God's enduring love, liberation and the risen Savior. Joy is grounded in these acts rather than treated as a condition that earns divine acceptance.|Psalm-like thanks develops into good news for captives and the poor, then resurrection testimony. These distinct reasons give the repeated call to rejoice more content than a bare command to be happy.|The question about waiting functions as an invitation to participate. Mourning becoming dancing supplies a concrete image of rescue; it need not deny a grieving believer space to lament.|Praise;Deliverance;Resurrection;Joy|Psalm 118:24;Isaiah 61:1;Psalm 30:11|||9,7,8

expanded-breakthrough-red-rocks-worship|The weary singer asks the merciful Father and King Jesus for restoration. God's power and continuing presence are sound grounds for trust, but the declared victory here is not tied to a defined promise.|Scars, brokenness and weariness give the prayer a personal setting. Mountains, seas and falling fire accumulate rescue images without explaining the cross or the nature of the expected breakthrough.|The movement from quiet need to forceful declaration is clear. Repeating an undefined breakthrough leaves its meaning open to the singer's desired outcome, which the text never identifies.|Prayer;Restoration;Divine presence;Hope|Psalm 34:18;1 John 5:14;Isaiah 43:2|There will be victory here|Trust in God's final victory does not establish that a chosen problem must resolve in this gathering. The text should identify what promise supports that immediate expectation.|7,5,7

expanded-echo-holy-red-rocks-worship|The Lord receives glory, power and exclusive worship among heaven's gathered host. The scene draws on biblical throne worship; its imaginative details describe participation rather than independent revelation about heaven.|Holiness, divine majesty and eternal praise stay central. The text develops the worship scene through gathering, shared voices and final sight of glory, but gives little explanation of redemption.|The echo and symphony images connect individual praise with a larger assembly. The claim that the anthem was always within the singer is poetic familiarity, not a developed teaching about preexistent souls.|Holiness;Heavenly worship;Divine majesty;Eternal praise|Isaiah 6:3;Revelation 4:8;Revelation 5:13|||9,6,8

expanded-something-has-to-break-red-rocks-worship|Asking the Spirit to expose lies and put wrongs right is a sound petition. The bridge goes further by asserting that an unspecified result will happen immediately, without identifying a divine promise for that timing.|The short text concentrates on change, leading and deliverance. It says little about what must change beyond lies and wrongs, and offers no account of Christ's saving work.|The central phrase is memorable but its indefinite subject never becomes concrete. Repetition intensifies the expectation more than it develops the prayer's meaning.|Prayer;Renewal;Holy Spirit;Deliverance|Psalm 139:23;John 16:13;1 John 5:14|You will do it right now|The text supplies no specific promise establishing this immediate timetable. Prayer for change should remain submission to the Spirit rather than certainty about a desired moment.|6,4,6

expanded-i-know-a-name-elevation-worship|Jesus is named as the risen Savior, ruler over death and fulfillment of the serpent's defeat. The repeated every-time claim about things leaving graves turns those truths into an unrestricted outcome the verses do not establish.|Waves, nail scars, keys, resurrection and conquest give the song substantial biblical material. Its strongest claims concern Christ's accomplished victory; the refrain blurs that accomplishment with repeated present manifestations.|The name motif gathers the images around Jesus. The shift from his unique resurrection to something emerging whenever the singer calls is the main point where the language overreaches.|Resurrection;Christ's authority;Salvation;Victory over evil|Acts 4:12;Revelation 1:18;Genesis 3:15|Every time I call Your Name|Christ's authority does not make every spoken invocation produce a resurrection, healing or visible breakthrough. The absolute repetition needs qualification by God's will and the actual promise being trusted.|7,7,7

expanded-son-of-suffering-bethel-music|The innocent Son truly shares human grief, suffers and gives freedom through his cross. Speaking of God weeping and bleeding is coherent when understood of the incarnate Son in his humanity.|Incarnation, compassion, mercy and atonement ground the praise in specific actions. The wounds answer the charge that God is distant, while the bridge connects his suffering to the believer's freedom.|Blood, tears and wounds sustain a clear central image. The healing phrase should be read with the song's saving context rather than as a guarantee that believers immediately escape all illness.|Incarnation;Compassion;Atonement;Christ's suffering|Isaiah 53:3;Hebrews 4:15;1 Peter 2:24|||9,8,8

expanded-ain-t-no-grave-bethel-music|The cross, Christ's resurrection and the believer's future bodily rising ground the victory over fear. The descent narrative and a trumpet at Jesus' own resurrection add details not established by the cited resurrection accounts.|The text moves from shame and fear to the Lamb's death and shared resurrection hope. These are concrete saving claims, though the conquest story combines distinct biblical images too freely.|Personified shame and fear make the opening vivid, and the change from Christ's grave to the believer's grave gives the refrain direction. The trumpet imagery confuses Christ's resurrection with the final resurrection.|Resurrection;Atonement;Freedom from fear;Eternal hope|Acts 2:24;Revelation 1:18;1 Corinthians 15:52|And He went on down to hell|Christ's authority over death is explicit in Scripture, but a detailed mission to retrieve keys from hell is not stated by these passages. The song also places final-trumpet imagery into Jesus' own resurrection scene.|7,8,7

expanded-one-thing-remains-bethel-music|Enduring divine love sustains confidence through trials and death. The bridge's paid debt provides a redemptive basis for assurance, rather than claiming that love means the absence of difficulty.|The text develops one theme through mountains, change, fear and inseparability. Its range is deliberately narrow, with the bridge adding more theological content than the repeated chorus alone.|The recurring negative statements emphasize constancy clearly. Their repetition is purposeful assurance, while the bridge explains why the singer trusts that love to endure.|Divine love;Assurance;Perseverance;Redemption|Romans 8:38;Romans 8:39;Psalm 136:1|||9,6,8

expanded-our-father-bethel-music|The prayer honors the Father and submits earth's life to his kingdom and will. The concluding kingdom, power and glory belong to God, keeping the petition centered on divine rule rather than human control.|This is a selected portion of the Lord's Prayer, concentrating on holiness, kingdom and obedience. It has a clear biblical focus without attempting to reproduce every petition.|The repeated heaven-coming request restates the desire for God's will on earth. Its meaning comes from the preceding prayer, not from a claim that a particular atmosphere proves heaven has arrived.|Prayer;God's kingdom;Obedience;Divine glory|Matthew 6:9;Matthew 6:10;Matthew 6:13|||9,6,8

expanded-the-blood-bethel-music|Christ's blood is the basis of forgiveness and acceptance, explicitly opposed to earning or performance. Changed conduct follows the encounter with Christ rather than purchasing the cleansing it describes.|The verses connect conversion, removed shame and inward change with justification and freely given grace. The bridge explains the refrain instead of leaving blood as an unexplained devotional symbol.|Before-and-after contrasts make the testimony concrete. Repeated thanks is supported by the bridge's direct account of grace and by the described changes in speech and conduct.|Atonement;Grace;Justification;New life|Ephesians 1:7;Ephesians 2:8;2 Corinthians 5:17|||9,8,8

expanded-highlands-song-of-ascent-hillsong-united|God remains faithful in valleys as on mountains. The slain Shepherd and empty grave ground access to grace in Christ's work.|The journey imagery develops perseverance, forgiveness and resurrection hope rather than promising an uninterrupted ascent into success.|Mountains become both obstacles and places of praise. The upward river is vivid resurrection poetry, though its layered geography needs attentive singing.|Perseverance;Grace;Resurrection|Psalm 23:4;John 10:11;Romans 8:39|||9,8,8

expanded-whole-heart-hold-me-now-hillsong-united|Forgiveness and freedom are credited to grace and the risen Christ. Sin's lost hold describes broken dominion, not an assertion of sinless perfection.|Clay, rock, wounds, chains and resurrection connect restoration with redemption. Surrender answers grace rather than buying acceptance.|The refrain develops from a broken heart to healing and forgiveness. Some copied wording is awkward, but the main images cohere around being upheld.|Grace;Forgiveness;Resurrection|Psalm 40:2;Romans 6:14;Ephesians 1:7|||9,7,7

expanded-as-you-find-me-hillsong-united|God meets undeserving sinners, and the bridge insists that his love transforms them. Acceptance is not permission to remain unchanged.|Failure, surrender, grace and Christ's scars give the testimony substance. The before-being-lost language expresses initiating love through an intentionally compressed paradox.|The opening contrasts make instability concrete, while the bridge resolves the tension between being loved as found and needing change.|Grace;Repentance;Divine love|Romans 5:8;Ephesians 1:4;Titus 2:12|||9,7,8

expanded-know-you-will-hillsong-united|God keeps his promises and preserves Christ's church. Confidence concerns his redemptive purpose, not certainty about the singer's preferred escape route.|Eden, Exodus, Jordan and the empty grave place present uncertainty inside a larger saving story, with final praise as its horizon.|The unknown-how and known-faithfulness contrast gives the refrain a clear argument. The biblical journey images provide its strongest explanation.|Providence;Perseverance;Redemption|Matthew 16:18;Isaiah 43:2;Philippians 1:6|||9,7,8

expanded-echoes-till-we-see-the-other-side-hillsong-united|Redemption is explicitly in Jesus' blood, and praise anticipates his kingdom. Felt changes in atmosphere do not establish a timetable for worldwide renewal.|The saving opening anchors images of dawn, awakening and resurrection. Repeated dancing and anticipation receive less explanation than the redemption claim.|Earth echoing heaven is a coherent praise image. The feeling-based prediction that darkness ends soon is less precise than the stated gospel ground.|Redemption;Hope;Praise|Ephesians 1:7;Romans 13:12;Revelation 21:4|I've got a feeling|An inward feeling does not establish how soon a trial, spiritual darkness or the present age will end. Hope rests on Christ's promises.|8,6,7

expanded-scandal-of-grace-hillsong-united|The innocent Jesus dies in the sinner's place and cleanses through his blood. His strength sustains life amid continuing trouble.|Substitution, mercy, defeat of death and imitation of Christ connect salvation with discipleship rather than stopping at pardon.|The scandal image expresses undeserved grace, while the cross teaches a changed life. Describing sin as dead concerns its defeated claim, not harmlessness.|Atonement;Grace;Discipleship|1 Peter 3:18;1 Corinthians 15:55;Ephesians 5:2|||9,8,8

expanded-not-today-hillsong-united|The cross and empty tomb ground confidence against evil. The absolute refusal of future fear overstates the believer's present freedom from struggle.|Christ's victory is connected to active praise and resistance. Singing is a response to that victory, not the act that creates it.|Direct speech to the enemy gives the song force, but repeated never-again language can obscure the continuing need for vigilance.|Christ's victory;Spiritual conflict;Courage|Colossians 2:15;James 4:7;1 Peter 5:8|Not now not ever again|Christians still face temptation, fear and spiritual opposition. This resolve should not be treated as a promise that those struggles cannot return.|8,7,7

expanded-wonder-hillsong-united|New sight and new life are connected with following Jesus. The water image evokes baptism without explaining water itself as an independent saving power.|Light, grace, gospel and freedom develop a conversion perspective. The saving events behind those benefits remain largely implicit.|Colour and wilderness imagery communicate changed perception coherently. Repeated seeing and walking phrases move the response toward public discipleship.|New life;Discipleship;Grace|2 Corinthians 5:17;Romans 6:4;Ephesians 5:8|||8,6,8

expanded-say-the-word-hillsong-united|God's effective word creates and gives life; the incarnate Word fulfills promise through cross and grave. Trust attaches to divine speech.|Creation, prophecy, incarnation and completed redemption provide several concrete reasons for relying on God's promises rather than human declarations.|Writing, speech and holding fast form a sustained motif. The stone contrast should not imply that God's earlier revelation lacked love.|God's word;Incarnation;Redemption|Isaiah 55:11;John 1:14;John 19:30|||9,8,8

expanded-even-when-it-hurts-praise-song-hillsong-united|The singer seeks cleansing and sustaining love while continuing to suffer. Praise in pain is devotion, not proof that grief must disappear.|Weakness, lament, waiting and final life beyond death develop perseverance. Christ's saving work remains less explicit than the personal response.|Heavy mountains and ocean tears make distress tangible. The strongest colloquial comparison can distract from congregational prayer even though the lament itself is legitimate.|Lament;Perseverance;Praise|Habakkuk 3:18;Psalm 42:5;Romans 8:18|Even when it hurts like Hell|The phrase intensifies suffering through colloquial language. Congregations should assess its register and distraction without condemning honest lament or requiring cheerful emotions.|8,6,6

expanded-go-hillsong-united|The Father gives freedom through Jesus the Savior, and surrendered living follows that gift. Commitment is presented as response rather than payment.|Calling, truth, opened perception and witness give the repeated surrender practical direction, although the saving cross is not developed.|The give-and-go refrain is simple and consistent. The later opened-eyes image explains why the singer now offers life for God's glory.|Surrender;Discipleship;Witness|Romans 12:1;John 14:6;Matthew 5:16|||8,6,8

expanded-relentless-hillsong-united|God's persistent love brings redemption, believing hearts and freedom. Christ's self-giving life supports the refrain's assurance of grace.|The verses move from salvation to persevering care and public light. The bridge adds liberation and costly love to the repeated theme.|Carrying, covering and breaking darkness give the central adjective specific meaning. Repetition emphasizes constancy rather than developing many separate doctrines.|Divine love;Redemption;Perseverance|Romans 8:39;John 8:12;John 10:11|||9,6,8

expanded-follow-you-anywhere-passion|Jesus' substitution at the cross grounds trust and costly discipleship. His presence accompanies following rather than guaranteeing that obedience remains easy.|Rescue, redemption, guidance and surrender connect gratitude with the willingness to bear cost. The cross supplies the commitment's central reason.|The fire and refuge images clarify guidance and safety. Calling love easy is qualified by the bridge's willingness to follow whatever obedience costs.|Discipleship;Atonement;Trust|1 Peter 2:24;Luke 9:23;Psalm 119:105|||9,7,8

expanded-fall-like-rain-passion|The prayer honors the Spirit and offers life to God. Rain describes desired renewal; it need not imply that the indwelling Spirit is absent.|Sacrifice, reordered desire, enduring fellowship and awe develop a focused prayer. Redemption receives less explanation than presence and worship.|Open hands and rain form accessible images of surrender and reception. The verses define the repeated request through friendship and lasting devotion.|Holy Spirit;Surrender;Prayer|Psalm 27:4;Romans 12:1;Ephesians 5:18|||8,6,8

expanded-the-jesus-way-phil-wickham|Enemy-love, forgiveness and endurance follow Jesus' bearing of sin. Choosing discipleship is a response to his saving work, not a claim to earn heaven.|Concrete situations of insult, need, persecution and death make obedience specific. The cross and eternal home ground costly moral commitments.|Parallel conditional statements make the ethical demands memorable. Their force should encourage courageous love without requiring people to remain within preventable abuse.|Discipleship;Enemy-love;Forgiveness|Matthew 5:44;1 Peter 2:24;Romans 12:21|||9,8,8

expanded-doxology-amen-phil-wickham|Praise is explicitly offered to Father, Son and Spirit, and the added stanza names the risen Christ as Savior and conqueror.|The traditional doxology is expanded by resurrection victory. This supplies a concrete saving reason for the repeated communal affirmation.|The added amen refrain functions as assent rather than filler. The second stanza develops the original universal call to praise.|Trinity;Resurrection;Praise|Matthew 28:19;1 Corinthians 15:57;Psalm 150:6|||9,7,9

expanded-at-your-name-phil-wickham|The Lord of creation receives exclusive praise, and the bridge explicitly confesses Jesus as God. Divine authority is the controlling theme.|Mountains, oceans, angels and creation describe the reach of God's majesty. The identity confession deepens a song otherwise concentrated on acclamation.|Personified creation and repeated naming form a coherent praise scene. Shouting is the singer's response, not a mechanism that activates divine power.|Christ's deity;Creation;Praise|John 1:1;Psalm 29:3;Psalm 96:11|||9,6,8

expanded-1000-names-phil-wickham|Jesus is confessed as incarnate divine glory, risen Lamb and true God. Father-language expresses care without explicitly denying the personal distinction of Father and Son.|Creator, second Adam, servant, king and conqueror accumulate substantial biblical identity claims. The bridge explains the wonder expressed in the chorus.|The large numbers are poetic abundance, not a literal inventory. The many titles remain anchored by naming Jesus and recalling incarnation and resurrection.|Christ's deity;Incarnation;Resurrection|Hebrews 1:3;1 Corinthians 15:45;Revelation 5:5|||9,8,8

expanded-the-king-is-in-the-room-phil-wickham|Jesus alone receives allegiance and worship. The claim that his presence forces immediate freedom from every fear needs distinction from his final victory.|Kingship, changed lives and salvation supply concrete themes. The text says less about the cross or the means of that salvation.|Doors, crowns and an occupied room form a clear royal scene. Enthroning language means acknowledging Christ's reign, not creating his authority.|Christ's reign;Worship;Deliverance|Philippians 2:10;Matthew 18:20;John 16:33|Fear has to flee|Christ's presence supports courage without guaranteeing instant emotional relief for every worshiper. Ongoing fear does not demonstrate that Jesus is absent.|8,6,7

expanded-praise-you-anywhere-brandon-lake|Praise is offered during darkness, waiting and suffering because God is faithful. Biblical rescues inspire worship but do not guarantee identical escapes.|Prison, fire, valleys and remembered promises give endurance concrete settings. Waiting for an answer helps qualify the energetic victory imagery.|The recurring anywhere confession holds the varied scenes together. Prison-door language should describe trustful worship rather than a noise-driven mechanism for rescue.|Perseverance;Praise;Trust|Acts 16:25;Habakkuk 3:18;Psalm 34:1|||8,7,8

expanded-that-s-who-i-praise-brandon-lake|The slain Lamb and risen Messiah receive praise. Individual biblical deliverances are applied too directly when the singer declares that fire cannot burn them.|David, Paul, Moses and Daniel provide examples of faith, and the final commitment to love like Jesus gives the praise ethical direction.|The rapid biblical catalogue is memorable but compresses distinct stories and promises. Praise is not a technique that automatically recreates Jericho's outcome.|Praise;Faith;Christ's victory|Daniel 3:18;Revelation 5:12;Hebrews 11:36|It won't burn me though|Daniel's faithful companions trusted God even if he did not rescue them. Their deliverance does not promise that every faithful singer escapes bodily harm.|7,8,7

expanded-count-em-brandon-lake|Christ's empty tomb and authority ground the holiness refrain. Universal bowing is biblical; universal saving possession of every heart is a different claim.|Healing accounts, resurrection, prophecy and conversion give the praise considerable content. Modern miracle testimony is not independently verified by including it in a song.|Counting the uncountable is an effective organizing image. Competitive scorekeeping and broad claims about every heart need more precision than the miracle catalogue supplies.|Christ's authority;Resurrection;Holiness|Philippians 2:10;John 9:6;Revelation 19:15|every heart will be Yours|Every knee bowing does not establish that every person will be saved. The line needs the distinction between universal submission and saving union with Christ.|7,8,7

expanded-tear-off-the-roof-brandon-lake|The healings in Jesus' ministry demonstrate his compassion and power. The singer's declaration that healing need not wait turns narrative examples into an immediate universal promise.|The roof and garment episodes supply identifiable biblical scenes, and Christ's blood is named. The saving meaning of the cross remains less developed than physical healing.|The linked rescue scenes make the appeal vivid. Unrestricted healing and no-ceiling language intensify expectation without supplying a promise governing each present request.|Healing;Faith;Christ's authority|Mark 2:5;Mark 5:34;2 Corinthians 12:9|I don't have to wait to get the healing|The cited healings do not guarantee immediate recovery to everyone who expresses sufficient determination. Faith depends on Christ, not on setting his timetable.|6,6,7

expanded-house-of-miracles-brandon-lake|Jesus' reign and resurrection ground hope, and the opening submits to his final say. The blood-in-veins metaphor blurs spiritual participation with physical identity.|Worship, healing, resurrection and providence are linked, but the song repeatedly declares outcomes without explaining the scope of God's promises.|The house image unifies the gathering's purpose. The bodily blood metaphor is less precise than the clear act of bringing needs to Jesus.|Resurrection;Prayer;Providence|Romans 8:28;Romans 8:11;Ephesians 1:7|Your blood runs through our veins|Believers receive life through Christ's sacrifice and Spirit; his physical blood does not circulate in their bodies. Use the line as dependence imagery, not biological or divine identity.|7,6,7

expanded-i-believe-charity-gayle|The cross, bodily resurrection, Christ's return and the church's preservation ground faith. Healing language belongs within that saving context rather than guaranteeing present immunity.|The bridge develops new birth, freedom, mission and final sight of Christ, substantially expanding the opening confession of faithfulness.|The repeated belief statement gains specific content as the song progresses. Sea and foundation images support trust rather than supplying new saving promises.|Atonement;Resurrection;Christ's return|1 Corinthians 15:20;Matthew 16:18;Revelation 7:9|||9,8,8

expanded-endless-praise-charity-gayle|Jesus is worshiped as Lord, King and worthy Lamb in the heavenly assembly. The song looks toward communion with him beyond this life.|Holiness, divine faithfulness and final worship are developed through the throne scene. The Lamb's worth is central, though the saving sacrifice is largely implicit.|Repeated holiness and worthiness function as acclamation. Joining heaven's song gives the repetition a clear communal and future-facing purpose.|Holiness;Eternal hope;Heavenly worship|Revelation 4:8;Revelation 5:12;Revelation 22:4|||9,6,8

expanded-new-name-written-down-in-glory-charity-gayle|Jesus initiates rescue from shame, blindness and bondage. New creation and faith describe the changed believer rather than salvation through positive self-description.|Conversion, assurance and identity in Christ develop across the testimony. The saving cross receives less direct explanation than the transformation's effects.|The new-name motif coheres with the new-creation confession. The I-Am wordplay distinguishes God's naming authority from the singer's received identity.|New creation;Assurance;Faith|2 Corinthians 5:17;Luke 10:20;2 Corinthians 5:7|||9,7,8

expanded-you-have-made-me-glad-charity-gayle|Thanks answers God's love, faithfulness and works. Confidence in his sustaining strength should not be equated with escaping every temporal defeat.|Morning and night frame continuing remembrance, while the later trust stanza adds dependence to praise. Its theological focus remains deliberately narrow.|The recurring joy statement follows concrete reasons for thanksgiving. Repetition reinforces the psalm-like response rather than introducing new doctrinal material.|Thanksgiving;Faithfulness;Joy|Psalm 92:1;Psalm 92:4;Psalm 27:1|||9,6,8

expanded-we-need-a-miracle-charity-gayle|God's power and constancy warrant prayer, and the text asks for his will. Claiming every named request already accomplished exceeds that qualification.|Waiting, healing and breaking all become settings for God's glory. This broadens the prayer beyond success, though the already-done formula remains unresolved.|The miracle-maker refrain is clear, but the undefined request shifts between submission and certainty. Those are not interchangeable ways of describing prayer.|Prayer;Divine power;Submission|Ephesians 3:20;1 John 5:14;Luke 22:42|It's already done|Praying in Jesus' name is not assurance that every requested outcome is already accomplished. The song's own submission to God's will should govern this declaration.|7,6,7

expanded-name-above-all-names-charity-gayle|Christ's sufficient sacrifice, resurrection and reign ground his exalted name. The declared finished work governs the ongoing blood language.|Cross, torn veil, empty grave and enthronement develop a substantial account of access and victory through Jesus.|The central name refrain gathers the historical claims into praise. Continuing blood-flow language expresses enduring efficacy, not a repeated sacrifice.|Atonement;Resurrection;Christ's reign|Hebrews 10:14;Philippians 2:9;Hebrews 10:20|||9,8,8

expanded-because-of-jesus-charity-gayle|The covenant and Christ's blood ground forgiveness, righteousness and access to God. Transformation follows redemption rather than earning it.|Justification, sanctification, union with Christ and restorative mercy supply concrete content for the praise and testimony.|The recurring because statement provides a clear causal center. The verses explain both acceptance before God and the changed life that follows.|Justification;Sanctification;Union with Christ|Ephesians 1:7;Galatians 2:20;Hebrews 10:19|||9,9,8

expanded-echo-in-jesus-name-charity-gayle|Jesus' authority and victory are rightly confessed. Extending his miraculous authority to every singer without qualification overstates the commission and present healing promises.|Redemption, mercy and conquest appear alongside miracle accounts. The refrain concentrates on present declarations rather than explaining salvation through the cross.|The echo motif makes delegated dependence the stated aim. Repeated assertions of healing blur requesting God's action with declaring every desired result achieved.|Christ's authority;Healing;Deliverance|Matthew 28:18;1 John 5:14;2 Corinthians 12:9|the keys to do the same|The church's commission does not mean every Christian can reproduce every miracle at will. Christ remains sovereign over gifts, healing and the manner of their exercise.|7,7,7

expanded-living-in-the-overflow-charity-gayle|God's sovereignty, grace and the Spirit's work ground freedom. The universal claim of visible victory wherever singers go exceeds ordinary Christian experience.|The text connects praise with freedom and transformation, but overflow remains undefined and the miracle refrains add little explanation.|Overflow provides a consistent abundance image. Its open-ended meaning can absorb material or experiential expectations not established by the surrounding words.|Grace;Holy Spirit;Praise|Psalm 103:1;Ephesians 5:18;John 16:33|Everywhere we go we see|Faithful Christians encounter setbacks and suffering as well as visible deliverance. The statement should not make continuous outward success the test of the Spirit's presence.|7,5,7

expanded-amen-charity-gayle|The eternal Father and Jesus the saving Word receive worship. Christ's blood cleanses, and divine holiness and glory belong to him.|The second verse adds salvation through Jesus to the opening throne scene, giving the repeated affirmation a clear Christian confession.|Amen serves as communal assent to stated truths. Naming Jesus in the bridge clarifies the referent of the earlier acclamations.|Trinity;Atonement;Holiness|John 14:6;Revelation 5:13;Hebrews 13:8|||9,7,8

expanded-jubilee-maverick-city-music|Jesus is named as the hope of freedom and restoration. Isaiah's anointed-speaker language belongs first to his mission, then to the church's participation.|Captivity, blindness, healing and restored hope connect jubilee imagery with identifiable gospel scenes. They do not establish a personal entitlement to wealth.|The recurring liberation testimony ties the scenes together. Distinguishing Christ's fulfillment from the congregation's witness keeps the opening first-person voice clear.|Deliverance;Mission;Restoration|Luke 4:18;Luke 4:21;John 9:25|||8,7,8

expanded-refiner-maverick-city-music|Offering one's life and seeking purified motives are sound responses to God. The suggestion that God needs an offering requires a distinction from human dependence.|Refining fire, clean hands and a living sacrifice develop sanctification, though the prior saving work enabling that response remains implicit.|The fire image is sustained through cleansing and devotion. Being consumed describes surrender of sin and divided loyalties, not self-destruction.|Sanctification;Surrender;Purity|Romans 12:1;Malachi 3:3;Acts 17:25|If what You need|God does not lack resources supplied by worshipers. Offering life responds to his grace; it does not satisfy a deficiency in him.|8,6,7

expanded-communion-maverick-city-music|The song seeks intimate fellowship and received acceptance. The ground of that acceptance is not explained through Christ, faith or the cross.|Garden, renewed life and friendship develop relational devotion. The text supplies little account of how estranged sinners gain access to God.|Garden and breathing images make closeness tangible. The approval declaration needs a clearer referent than the experience of feeling known.|Fellowship;Divine presence;Acceptance|John 15:4;Ephesians 2:18;Romans 5:1|You've already approved of me|Acceptance with God rests on reconciliation through Christ, not simply on a feeling of closeness or a universal statement of approval.|7,5,7

expanded-such-an-awesome-god-maverick-city-music|Creation and sustaining care lead to explicit confession of Jesus' death and resurrection. Divine generosity is attached to these acts rather than mere admiration.|Holiness, mercy, providence and saving victory give the repeated greatness refrain concrete content. The final outpouring phrases are less specific.|The praise adjectives are supported by the sun, breath, cross and empty grave. These anchors keep the worship focused despite the open-ended ending.|Divine majesty;Providence;Resurrection|Acts 17:25;Acts 2:24;Psalm 145:8|||9,7,8

expanded-be-praised-maverick-city-music|The God who speaks creation into being also brings the spiritually dead to life.
